Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Vignette:
Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a bomb disposal technician. For over three decades, he had navigated the most hazardous situations with precision and calm. But everything changed on that fateful day when he was exposed to toxic chemicals while defusing a bomb. The memory of the incident still lingered vividly – the hissing sound of the chemical leak, the acrid smell that seared his nostrils, and the feeling of his skin burning as if on fire. In the months that followed, Kofi began to notice changes in himself. Loud noises would startle him, sending his heart racing and transporting him back to that moment when his life hung by a thread. He found himself scanning every room he entered, identifying potential escape routes before feeling comfortable enough to stay. His wife, Ama, would often catch him staring intently at their surroundings, his eyes darting from one corner to the next as if searching for an invisible threat. Kofi became increasingly uneasy when alone in a room or building. He would try to fill the silence with work, spending long hours at the office to avoid being alone with his thoughts. His colleagues began to notice the change in him – the way he would jump at every sudden noise, the way he would avoid physical examinations or hospital visits. Kofi was certain that hospitals were breeding grounds for germs and illnesses, and the antiseptic smell that lingered in the air only served as a harsh reminder of his own vulnerability. As time passed, Kofi's behaviors became more entrenched. He would overwork himself to exhaustion, not just to avoid being alone but also to keep his mind occupied. His relationships with Ama and their children began to suffer – they felt like they were losing him to the all-consuming fog of anxiety that had taken up residence in their home. Ama tried to reassure Kofi that he was safe, that she was there for him, but her words offered little comfort. One day, while out on a job, Kofi's team responded to an emergency call at a local hospital. As they entered the building, the familiar antiseptic smell hit him like a punch to the gut. He felt his heart racing, his senses on high alert as he scanned the area for potential dangers. Suddenly, one of his teammates touched him unexpectedly, and Kofi's body reacted with alarm – his muscles tensed, his eyes scanning wildly for an escape route. It was then that Kofi realized he needed help. The memories of the traumatic event were no longer just memories but had become an integral part of his daily life. He couldn't shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge, waiting for the other shoe to drop. Ama noticed the change in him too – the way he would hesitate before leaving the house, the way he would freeze at every sudden noise. With a deep sense of trepidation, Kofi finally sought help. As he sat in the therapist's office, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking into another trap, another situation where his safety could be compromised. But something about the calm demeanor of the therapist put him at ease – just enough to allow him to share his story, to relive the memories that had haunted him for so long. Kofi's eyes locked onto the therapist as he spoke, his voice barely above a whisper. "I'm scared," he said, the words tumbling out like a confession. "I'm scared of losing myself completely, of becoming trapped in this never-ending cycle of fear and anxiety." The therapist nodded, her expression compassionate, and for the first time in months, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to navigate his way back to a life free from the suffocating grip of trauma.
